clinicalPearls: A form of pigmentary mosaicism with streaks, whorls and patches of hypopigmentation following the lines of Blaschko
Best regarded as a cutaneous marker of underlying somatic mosaicism rather than a single disease entity
Extracutaneous anomalies, especially of the central nervous system (seizures, developmental delay), eyes and musculoskeletal system, occur in a substantial proportion
The hypopigmentation is usually present from birth or appears in infancy and is best appreciated under Wood's lamp
It is not inherited in a simple Mendelian fashion; most cases arise from postzygotic mosaicism (chromosomal or genetic)
The pattern is the negative image of the hyperpigmented streaks seen in some other mosaic disorders
Management is supportive, with developmental, neurological and ophthalmological assessment to detect and treat associated anomalies
reference.pathophysiology: Hypomelanosis of Ito is a manifestation of cutaneous mosaicism in which two genetically distinct clonal populations of cells coexist, arising from postzygotic events such as chromosomal mosaicism, aneuploidy or somatic mutation. The Blaschko-linear distribution reflects the dorsoventral migration and proliferation of these clones during embryogenesis, with the hypopigmented streaks corresponding to clones bearing reduced melanocyte function or number. Because the same mosaic clones can populate non-cutaneous tissues, affected individuals may have anomalies of the nervous system, eyes and skeleton. It is therefore not a distinct disease with a single gene but a descriptive pattern signalling underlying genetic mosaicism, and karyotyping of skin and blood may reveal chromosomal differences.
additionalDifferentials: Linear and whorled naevoid hypermelanosis (the pigmentary opposite)
additionalInvestigations: Wood's lamp examination to delineate the hypopigmented pattern
Karyotyping/chromosomal microarray of skin fibroblasts and blood to detect mosaicism
Developmental and neurological assessment, with electroencephalography if seizures occur
Neuroimaging where central nervous system involvement is suspected
Skeletal and dental evaluation as indicated
redFlags: Seizures or developmental regression indicating central nervous system involvement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is determined by the extent of extracutaneous involvement rather than the skin change, which itself is benign and may become less conspicuous with age. When neurological or other systemic anomalies are absent the outlook is excellent; associated CNS disease is the main source of long-term morbidity.
pitfalls: Treating it as a purely cosmetic skin finding and failing to assess for neurological and other anomalies
Confusing it with the hypopigmented stage of incontinentia pigmenti
Relying on blood karyotype alone, when mosaicism may be detectable only in skin
Assuming Mendelian inheritance and giving inappropriate recurrence-risk counselling
management: Recognise the skin change as benign and requiring no specific dermatological treatment, directing care instead at detecting extracutaneous involvement
Assess neurodevelopment and manage seizures with antiseizure medication and developmental support where present
Arrange ophthalmological, skeletal and dental evaluation to detect associated anomalies
Obtain chromosomal microarray or karyotyping of skin fibroblasts and blood to characterise the underlying mosaicism
Provide neuroimaging and electroencephalography when central nervous system involvement is suspected
Offer genetic counselling, noting that most cases arise from postzygotic mosaicism rather than simple Mendelian inheritance
Coordinate long-term follow-up through paediatrics, neurology and clinical genetics
